title: Introduction to Finality

jokes.text: I miss Troy. Wrong, and stop guessing that.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what cellular mitosis is — a legitimate biology study question.
jokes.punchline: A student answers 'I miss Troy,' which is not an answer to the question at all, and the teacher curtly shoots it down with 'Wrong, and stop guessing that' — implying this is a repeated occurrence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold-open joke. The economy is superb — in four words it establishes Troy's absence, the group's emotional state, AND gets a sharp callback-style corrective from the teacher. The 'stop guessing that' implies it's been said multiple times, which layers character grief onto comedy brilliantly.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Teacher
dialogue.line: What is the primary function of mitochondria?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Student
dialogue.line: I miss Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Teacher
dialogue.line: That's... not correct. And frankly, I'm starting to think you're not actually answering the questions anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Student
dialogue.line: I miss Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Teacher
dialogue.line: This is the seventh time this semester you've given that exact answer. To completely different questions. About completely different topics.

jokes.text: Did someone say 'sexy construction worker'? Ooh! Stay on target.
jokes.setup: Annie says 'Can we stay on target?' — a plea for focus during biology study.
jokes.punchline: Dean Pelton bursts in dressed as a sexy construction worker, mishearing or willfully interpreting 'stay on target' as an invitation, then echoes the phrase himself.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton costume gag. The character integration is high — only the Dean would do this — and the self-echo ('Stay on target') is a nice structural touch. But it's a well-worn Dean bit at this point in the series, slightly coasting on the character's established absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed won't play in the Dreamatorium.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I mean, he refuses to participate in the postmodern metanarrative construct that is the Dreamatorium.

jokes.text: I'm dressed like this because I'm building to big news.
jokes.setup: The Dean is visibly dressed as a sexy construction worker with no apparent explanation.
jokes.punchline: He offers the rationale that his outfit is a 'building' pun for his upcoming announcement — a groan-worthy wordplay delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The Dean's total commitment to a terrible pun as the justification for his elaborate costume is very on-brand. Works because it retroactively makes the absurdity feel 'logical' in his mind, which deepens his character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I heard about Abed and Troy. That's a real shame. You know what? I'm going to dress up as a priest and give them some spiritual guidance.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Wait, they're not breaking up? They're just having an argument? Well, I'm already in the outfit. I'm going with it.

jokes.text: We should both sign, we're 50-50 partners. / But there's only one dotted line, so... / Oh, Pierce can... / Me. / Hey! I paid for it. / There'd be no 'it' if I hadn't done the work.
jokes.setup: The Dean announces Shirley's Sandwiches will occupy the cafeteria kiosk — an apparent triumph.
jokes.punchline: Immediately the partnership collapses into petty squabbling over a single signature line, with both trying to shove the other out in the same breath they're celebrating.
jokes.explanation: Solid situational comedy. The speed at which celebration turns to conflict is funny, and both characters' logic is perfectly in-character. Not particularly original but well-executed within the episode's plot machinery.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm here to deliver some building news.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: And I'm dressed for the occasion because I wanted to... construct my appearance around the message.

jokes.text: My goodness, this molehill is becoming a mountain.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce are already in a heated dispute just seconds after their joint business victory.
jokes.punchline: The Dean delivers a blandly understated idiom to describe what is clearly an immediate and total breakdown of a business partnership — then exits to 'put together an alpine costume' to match the mountain metaphor.
jokes.explanation: The Dean's exit line and self-contained costume callback (alpine = mountain) is a clever layered gag. The understatement is mild but the commitment to the bit (changing into an alpine costume) makes it funnier than the line alone.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We should both sign as 50-50 partners.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm going to claim sole ownership.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What?! Pierce, we agreed!

jokes.text: You work it out while I put together an alpine costume.
jokes.setup: Dean just said 'this molehill is becoming a mountain.'
jokes.punchline: He announces he's going to change into an alpine costume to match his own metaphor — prioritizing his costume change over the actual conflict.
jokes.explanation: This is the better Dean joke of the pair. It rewards attentive viewers who caught the mountain metaphor and delivers a character truth: the Dean cares more about his outfit matching the moment than resolving any actual conflict. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Isn't therapy just a way for people to avoid actually changing?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh wow, you're really setting yourself up there, aren't you?

jokes.text: Get involved. / No. / I am here to replace my fake bachelor's so I can get back to my life as a lawyer.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce are arguing; someone appeals to Jeff to mediate.
jokes.punchline: Jeff flatly refuses and delivers a self-serving speech about not sacrificing his interests — which is played as a character flaw the show is explicitly calling out.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff selfishness, well-executed but fairly standard for his character arc at this point. Functions more as thematic setup than a pure laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: There's no such thing as bad press.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Leonard, that only works if people know who you are. You could walk into a Starbucks covered in blood holding a chainsaw and the barista would just think you were quirky.

jokes.text: That's you just now. [shows mirror or points]
jokes.setup: Jeff lectures about not sacrificing his interests and how 'nobody else is sacrificing their interests.'
jokes.punchline: Annie or another character holds up the metaphorical mirror — 'That's you just now' — to show Jeff he's doing exactly what he's criticizing others for.
jokes.explanation: Functional irony beat. The callback structure is clean — immediately reversing Jeff's speech back on him — but the moment doesn't transcend the formula.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm making a human centipede out of the study group.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... not ideal.

jokes.text: His what? He's been feeling vulnerable having lost Troy to the air conditioning repair school, so he's gonna let me practice my psych skills on him. Give me some credit. What's the worst that could happen?
jokes.setup: Britta casually announces she is going to do therapy on Abed.
jokes.punchline: 'What's the worst that could happen?' — a classic TV tee-up line the show immediately acknowledges as such.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the meta-joke that follows. Works as a deliberate ironic tee-up but functions mainly as a prompt for the next punchline rather than standing alone.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I wasn't listening. What did you say?

dialogue.speaker: AC Teacher
dialogue.line: Were you even paying attention?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, not really. I've been thinking about Abed all morning.

jokes.text: Classic tee-up. Shut up, Leonard, I know about your crooked wang. No such thing as bad press.
jokes.setup: Britta says 'What's the worst that could happen?' — a classic TV dramatic irony setup.
jokes.punchline: Leonard calls it a 'classic tee-up' (meta commentary), Britta silences him with a personal insult about his anatomy, and Leonard cheerfully replies 'No such thing as bad press.'
jokes.explanation: Three-part joke that escalates beautifully. Leonard's meta-commentary is sharp; Britta's anatomical shutdown is shockingly specific; and Leonard's PR-speak response ('No such thing as bad press') is perfectly absurd character logic. Each beat tops the last. Leonard's 'bad press' line alone is quotable. This is well above average for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: You are the one spoken of in the ancient prophecy. You will bring balance to the air conditioning system.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I have feelings for Britta.

jokes.text: Britta arrives at Abed's apartment and sees something alarming — 'This can't be good.'
jokes.setup: Britta arrives to do therapy on Abed, expecting to find him simply sad.
jokes.punchline: Whatever she sees (inferred: Abed has built an elaborate alternate-timeline scenario inside the apartment, possibly in costume or character) prompts a deadpan 'This can't be good.'
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man reaction beat. Works because we share Britta's dawning dread before we even understand what she's seeing. The simplicity of the line amplifies the visual reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean Laybourne
dialogue.line: A great darkness is coming. The signs are all around us. Only one of pure heart can prevent the catastrophe.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Have you seen Abed?

jokes.text: Hey, Troy. We boring you? / I miss my friends. / He misses his friends. / Aw.
jokes.setup: Troy is in an intense air conditioning repair lecture about capillary tubes and compressor valves.
jokes.punchline: Called out for daydreaming, Troy doesn't deny it and says 'I miss my friends.' The room of hardened repairmen all respond with a sincere collective 'Aw' — softness from unexpected sources.
jokes.explanation: The humor comes from tonal contrast: an intense, masculine technical school dissolves instantly into collective sweetness because one man misses his friends. 'He misses his friends / Aw' is a perfect quick beat — the echo structure amplifies the bathos.

dialogue.speaker: Vice Dean
dialogue.line: I foresee a great darkness descending upon Greendale. The walls will crumble, the very foundations of our institution will shake, and chaos will reign supreme.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's cool. Hey, have you seen Abed? I miss hanging out with that guy.

jokes.text: The Sun Chamber. A shameful relic from a savage chapter of our history. Repairmen would duel each other inside, losers succumbing to heat exhaustion, or worse.
jokes.setup: The air conditioning repair school is played as a secretive, mystic, ritualistic order.
jokes.punchline: The 'shameful relic' is a room where repairmen historically dueled to the death via... heat exhaustion from broken air conditioners. The specificity of the mundane danger is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Community's AC repair school arc is one of the show's most committed absurdist conceits — taking a banal trade school and treating it as a warrior cult. This line is a good example of that sustained absurdism: 'succumbing to heat exhaustion, or worse' is delivered with the gravity of a war crime.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My destiny is clear. I am meant to repair men, to restore their broken spirits and guide them toward enlightenment.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You mean like fixing their cars?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, Abed, it's about spiritual renewal and—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because you're going to be an air conditioning repair man.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? No. I'm talking about a higher calling.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool. You start Monday.

jokes.text: Troy, there is a prophesy... I'm ashamed to confess that I once thought that this might be me. Now I realize that it's you. You are the true repairman, Troy. You fix not only air conditioners, but the men who fix them.
jokes.setup: Grandiose prophecy being delivered about the 'true repairman.'
jokes.punchline: 'It's a trade school. It's a two-year degree in boxes that make rooms cold.' — Troy internally (or aloud) deflates the entire mythology.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of epic hero mythology with 'boxes that make rooms cold' is the comedic engine of the entire AC school subplot, and this is its purest expression. The deflation is perfectly timed — the prophecy speech is long enough to build genuine absurd momentum before Troy smashes it with mundane reality.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You're talking to Britta? That's a mistake.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Says the guy who's evil.

jokes.text: The true repairman will repair man.
jokes.setup: An elaborate mystic prophecy is being intoned about Troy's destiny.
jokes.punchline: The grand prophecy is literally just a pun: 'repair man' / 'repair man' — the mystical revelation is a wordplay joke delivered as cosmic truth.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The genius is structural: the entire AC school arc has been building toward a grand destiny prophecy, and the payoff is a pun so clean it barely registers as one on first hearing. 'Repair man' / 'repair man' — fixing air conditioners vs. fixing humanity. It's genuinely quotable, economical to the point of perfection, and funny on multiple levels (the absurdism of the cult + the wordplay + the deadpan delivery of an earnest pun as prophecy). Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You think you know me? You think you understand what I am? I am the darkness between the frames, the truth behind the fourth wall. And when this show ends, I'll be waiting in the spaces where reality bends.

jokes.text: I'm reading Chronicles of Riddick. Can you tell me that's a saner decision?
jokes.setup: Britta insists Abed talk to her instead of retreating into his inner dialogue, implying he's going crazy.
jokes.punchline: Abed deflects the sanity question by pointing out he's reading Chronicles of Riddick — implying that's also not sane.
jokes.explanation: Abed's self-awareness about pop culture quality as a sanity metric is on-brand and gets a solid chuckle. The logic is funny but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You don't actually want biology help, do you?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No, not really.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So why'd you lie about it?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Because I didn't want to hurt your feelings! But look how awkward this is now.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: ♪ I lied, I lied, I told a fib so wide! ♪ See? Terrible!

jokes.text: Because you think you're broken, you're gonna get diagnosed by someone who said her favorite superhero was X Man?
jokes.setup: Abed is considering letting Britta 'fix' him through amateur psychology.
jokes.punchline: He undermines Britta's credentials by citing 'X Man' — apparently she once named a singular, non-existent superhero as her favorite, which signals total comic book illiteracy.
jokes.explanation: Sharp character-specific dig. 'X Man' (singular) is a great joke for Community's reference-dense world — only someone with zero comic knowledge would say 'X Man' instead of 'an X-Man.' Works perfectly as Abed-logic to dismiss Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm free Tuesday afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not. I have a very important appointment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What appointment?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm going to go home and die.

jokes.text: When the world gets bad enough, the good go crazy. But the smart... They go bad.
jokes.setup: Abed is psychologically spiraling from Troy's absence and rationalizing a 'dark' response.
jokes.punchline: His 'dark' logic sounds villainous and profound but is actually just Abed doing a movie-villain monologue in his apartment — the gap between register and reality is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Abed's villain monologue delivered as emotional coping is very funny and fits his character perfectly. The line has genuine quotability and is a good distillation of the episode's dark-timeline conceit.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I have a law degree from Colombia. Not the country, the university. Well, actually it's a certificate I got online for $400, but it's from Colombia University online, which counts.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I used it to sue my own parents for my birth. Turns out I won. I'm now legally my own father.

jokes.text: Are you lying? / Hard to break the word 'yes' into lilting syllables? / Ye-es?
jokes.setup: Jeff asks if Annie is lying; she denies it with the same over-enunciated innocent voice.
jokes.punchline: Jeff calls out the affectation directly — 'Hard to break the word yes into lilting syllables?' — perfectly naming the comedic device she's using.
jokes.explanation: Jeff meta-commenting on Annie's comedic technique is clever and self-aware without being overly meta. The line 'Hard to break the word yes into lilting syllables' is sharp writing — it explains the joke while being the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, you're not paranoid. Nobody's out to get you.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's exactly what someone who's out to get me would say.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going back to studying biology now.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Biology? That's the study of life. Life is what they use to spy on you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I really need to focus on this exam.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Exams are just another way the government tracks your knowledge level.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, please. I'm begging you. Just... let me study.

jokes.text: A-ha! Crazy? Paranoid? Impotent? / Cellular... / Mitosis.
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to study; Shirley tells him to let Pierce cool down because Pierce can get 'crazy and paranoid.'
jokes.punchline: Pierce storms in mid-sentence, mishears the conversation, and accuses them of calling him impotent — escalating from paranoid to paranoid AND impotent. Jeff and Annie try to redirect with 'Cellular... Mitosis.'
jokes.explanation: Pierce's escalation from 'paranoid' to 'impotent' is a funny non-sequitur that reveals his insecurities. The 'Cellular... mitosis' deflection is a good running-gag callback to the biology exam pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: The Vice Dean was a man of many talents. He could negotiate a contract, he could lead a meeting, and apparently, he could inhale freon like it was going out of style. But you know what? At least he died doing what he loved. And that was... being really, really cold.

jokes.text: Obviously, Shirley has her counsel, and I get to dress like a judge.
jokes.setup: Pierce has demanded the dispute be settled in 'Greendale Court' — an apparently real thing.
jokes.punchline: The Dean announces the arrangement where the genuinely absurd part — that he 'gets to dress like a judge' — is delivered as the obvious and best part of this for him.
jokes.explanation: Dean Pelton's priorities being entirely about the costume is consistent and funny. 'I get to dress like a judge' as the obviously best feature of this arrangement is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Alan! Hey, man. I got this.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Actually, did you know that tennis scoring comes from clock faces? In medieval times, they used the 60-minute clock face and moved the hand a quarter turn for each point, which is why it goes 0, 15, 30, 45, and then game. It's called deuce when the score is tied at 40-40 because 'deuce' comes from the French 'deux,' meaning two, and—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, I don't got this.

jokes.text: I was born in a courtroom, sued it for my own placenta, and won.
jokes.setup: Pierce is boasting about his legal toughness before calling his lawyer.
jokes.punchline: He claims to have literally sued the courtroom of his birth for his own placenta — a brag so specific, absurd, and legally incoherent that it's a perfect Pierce-ism.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. It's perfectly Pierce: wealthy, litigious, nonsensical, and self-aggrandizing. The image of a baby suing a courtroom for its own placenta is irreducibly absurd in a way that could only come from this character. The escalation (born in a courtroom → sued it → for his OWN placenta → won) has perfect comedic architecture. Genuinely quotable and high on originality.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: You see, Pierce is like a cow. We milk him for all he's worth.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: And when he's all dried up, we send him to the glue factory.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, that's... that's disturbing.

jokes.text: May his breeze join the wind.
jokes.setup: Vice Dean Laybourne has died from inhaling a lethal dose of Freon.
jokes.punchline: The repairmen's funeral tribute is 'May his breeze join the wind' — a death eulogy structured exactly like a religious blessing but entirely in HVAC metaphor.
jokes.explanation: Five words that capture the entire comedic premise of the AC repair school subplot: a banal trade is treated as a sacred calling with its own spiritual vocabulary. 'May his breeze join the wind' is structurally perfect — it has the cadence and sincerity of 'may he rest in peace' but the content is HVAC poetry. Highly quotable, maximally economical, and original.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Go easy on me in court, okay?

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I'll be gentle. I promise I won't treat you like you're Lex Luthor's stunt double.

jokes.text: That's a rookie mistake. I'm sure it was a faulty valve. My first order as vice dean, have them replaced.
jokes.setup: Vice Dean Laybourne has just died from a 'faulty valve' Freon rupture.
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately questions how the best repairman in the school could make a 'rookie mistake' — implying foul play — then pivots to immediately consolidating power as the new Vice Dean.
jokes.explanation: The speed of the power grab following the death is darkly funny. Good structural joke — the suspicious framing followed by immediate self-promotion is a compressed villain arc.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I need help making an important judicial decision.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Should I be more like Judge Judy or Judge Dredd?

jokes.text: Pierce did you the biggest favor of your life. He hired a guy I've spent years fantasizing about stabbing in the... Sundance! Tango! Hey. Unh!
jokes.setup: Jeff is about to say he's fantasized about 'stabbing' Alan in something anatomical or violent.
jokes.punchline: Alan himself walks in, interrupting the sentence just before the vulgar/violent word, forcing Jeff to cover with enthusiastic non-sequiturs ('Sundance! Tango! Hey. Unh!').
jokes.explanation: 'Sundance! Tango! Hey. Unh!' as a desperate improvised greeting is a great physical comedy inference. The interrupted sentence structure is classic, but the specific words Jeff lands on are what elevate it above generic.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: In the darkest timeline, we use 'Britta' as a verb meaning to screw something up.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: As in, 'Oh no, I Britta'd it.'

jokes.text: Hawthorne's a cash cow, and old A-con here is tugging at that teat. That's money. / Money. / Please stop that.
jokes.setup: Alan explains why Pierce is a valuable client for the law firm.
jokes.punchline: The 'teat' metaphor delivered with relish, echoed by someone else, then 'Please stop that' — the rhythm of the discomfort is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Money' and 'Please stop that' creates a funny three-beat cringe moment. Alan's smarminess is well-drawn but the joke itself is functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You know what your problem is, Britta? You're afraid of commitment. You sabotage every relationship because deep down, you don't think you deserve to be happy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, what? That's not... I mean, that's not even close to—why are you doing a therapist voice?

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not doing a voice. I'm just being honest. You need to confront your abandonment issues.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, first of all, you're literally evil. Second, I'm the therapist here, remember? And third... am I actually doing that?

jokes.text: Full disclosure. I really want to be done by 4:00.
jokes.setup: Alan says 'full disclosure' as a legal/professional framing device for his threat.
jokes.punchline: Jeff mirrors the 'full disclosure' framing to reveal his only motivation is finishing by 4pm — turning a formal legal phrase into a confession of pure apathy.
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure ('Full disclosure' × 2) is tight and the content is a perfect Jeff characterization — his grand legal flourish reveals total self-interest. Economy is a strength here.

jokes.text: That's the Jeff wing basket I remember.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals his only interest is finishing by 4pm.
jokes.punchline: Alan recognizes Jeff's selfishness with fond nostalgia — 'That's the Jeff wing basket I remember' — implying this is exactly the Jeff he knew and exploited before.
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat. Alan's fondness for Jeff's worst qualities is a good dynamic, but 'wing basket' as a phrase is a little clunky — it doesn't land as cleanly as the idea deserves.

jokes.text: Hey, just go easy on Shirley. / Scout's honor, Sinéad O'Connor.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Alan to go easy on Shirley in the case.
jokes.punchline: Alan responds 'Scout's honor, Sinéad O'Connor' — using Shirley's name as a rhyme/pun with 'honor/O'Connor' in a mock-solemn promise.
jokes.explanation: A quick wordplay gag using the Sinéad O'Connor rhyme. Clever but lightweight — it's a name-drop pun that works phonetically more than comedically. Gets a small but real laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You're mediocre. Your psychology degree will be mediocre. Your career will be mediocre.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You know what else is mediocre? A frozen pizza slice left out for three days.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You're worse than that pizza slice.

jokes.text: Oy yay, oy yay. The Honorable Craig Pelton presiding. / First off, there's one decision I'll need your help making. / Judging Amy or Judge Judy?
jokes.setup: Court is convened; the Dean announces his first order of business as judge.
jokes.punchline: His first judicial act is soliciting opinions on which judge TV show persona he should adopt — 'Judging Amy or Judge Judy?' — a completely non-judicial concern.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dean Pelton logic — the 'one decision' he needs help with is entirely about his aesthetic presentation rather than the legal proceedings. 'Judging Amy or Judge Judy' is a good joke because Judging Amy is a deliberately 'wrong' answer (a drama, not a court show).

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You're like a pizza cutter. All the way around the pizza, never touching the pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's cool. I'd be a pizza cutter.

jokes.text: You say your name is Evil Abed, which does not throw me because I'm a therapist. So let's talk about evil.
jokes.setup: Abed has apparently presented himself to Britta as 'Evil Abed' from the darkest timeline.
jokes.punchline: Britta's response — 'which does not throw me because I'm a therapist' — is funny because she is absolutely thrown by it and barely a therapist at all.
jokes.explanation: Good Britta character work — her overconfidence is her comic flaw and it's deployed well here. The gap between her claim ('does not throw me') and the evident reality is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You're like Jim Belushi.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: I don't know. Nobody does. But everyone agrees it's bad.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: This timeline is now 47% darker.

jokes.text: Where I come from, his name is Lame Abed. / And you come from...? / The darkest timeline. Call it the Britta of timelines, where everything is the worst.
jokes.setup: Evil Abed mentions 'Lame Abed' and 'the darkest timeline.'
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'the Britta of timelines, where everything is the worst' — cementing 'Britta' as a synonym for worst/failure within the show's own universe.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode and arguably one of the most quotable lines Community ever produced. 'The Britta of timelines, where everything is the worst' is a perfect crystallization of the show's meta-character-comedy — it uses Britta as a noun/adjective in a way that is simultaneously an insult, a character truth, and a callback to a season-long running gag. It has zero wasted words, is completely character-specific, rewards long-time viewers, and introduced a phrase that Community fans genuinely adopted into their vocabulary. This is the 8.5+ benchmark for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: You're like a paint-by-numbers painting of a real person. You're like a Blockbuster Video in 2010. You're like a Nickelback album that somehow got worse. You're the human equivalent of a sequel nobody asked for, and not even a good one—you're like Die Hard 5.

jokes.text: Jeff has one arm there. Annie shot Pierce. Troy can't speak.
jokes.setup: Evil Abed is describing the darkest timeline to Britta.
jokes.punchline: The list of darkest-timeline horrors is delivered as a casual inventory — Jeff missing an arm, Annie shooting Pierce, Troy mute — with no elaboration, as if these are equally routine facts.
jokes.explanation: For fans of 'Remedial Chaos Theory,' this is a delightful callback delivered with casual menace. The economy of listing these horrors without reaction is what makes it work — Evil Abed treats them as mundane, which is funnier than dwelling on them.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm completely unprepared. Does anyone have any jokes?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Why did the Mexican drive a lowrider to the bank?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I don't know, why?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Because he wanted to make a de-pasta!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That doesn't even make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know, right? I don't really understand my own jokes.

jokes.text: I've crossed into your dark timeline, and I'm going to darken it. / How? / Tell me about your parents. / Um... no.
jokes.setup: Evil Abed delivers a villainous declaration that he's going to 'darken' this timeline.
jokes.punchline: Britta reflexively asks 'How?' and pivots to the most therapeutic question she knows — 'Tell me about your parents' — which deflates Evil Abed's menace completely, earning a flat 'Um... no.'
jokes.explanation: The deflation of evil-villain posturing by amateur therapy questions is a great structural joke. 'Tell me about your parents' is the most clichéd psychology question, and 'Um... no' is a perfect one-word shutdown. Good character specificity for both.

jokes.text: Miss Edison, do you recognize the baby in that picture? / That's Shirley's baby, Ben. / Would you think less of Shirley Bennett if she offered to 'sell Ben on Craigslist for a chance to bump it with Denzel'?
jokes.setup: Alan is cross-examining Annie in the mock trial about Shirley's character.
jokes.punchline: He pulls a quote from what is apparently Shirley's social media — she once joked about selling her baby on Craigslist for a date with Denzel Washington — delivered in full legalese.
jokes.explanation: The joke has two good layers: the specific absurdity of 'selling Ben on Craigslist for Denzel' (the specificity of Denzel is key), and the formal legal delivery of a messy informal social media post. Shirley's 'That was a joke for my cousin' and 'Damn those privacy settings' are good follow-up beats.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We are gathered here today for the sacred AC Awareness Ceremony, a tradition passed down through generations of Greendale leadership.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Now, I will perform the ancient ritual to ensure optimal air flow throughout our institution.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: First, we must acknowledge the spirits of the vents. Oh, mighty cooling forces, hear our plea.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We invoke the secret wind—the wind that flows only through the ducts of enlightened institutions.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: By the power vested in me as Dean, I hereby activate the sacred breath of Greendale.

jokes.text: That was a joke for my cousin. / Damn those privacy settings.
jokes.setup: Alan has just publicly read out Shirley's private social media post about selling her baby.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's defense is 'it was a joke for my cousin,' followed by the more revealing admission 'Damn those privacy settings' — which is funnier because it confirms the post is real.
jokes.explanation: 'Damn those privacy settings' is an economical, modern, and very relatable line that perfectly caps the joke. It shifts Shirley from defending the content to just being annoyed the post leaked — a funny priority inversion.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I invoke the deadly trial by combat!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: What?! No! Troy, what are you doing?!

jokes.text: Or perhaps she doesn't even love that baby because she spent most of last year not even knowing who the father is.
jokes.setup: Alan continues his attack on Shirley's character in court.
jokes.punchline: He raises Shirley's paternity storyline from Season 2 as a character attack — using real, humiliating personal history as a legal weapon in this ridiculous mock trial.
jokes.explanation: More of a plot callback than a crafted joke. Gets some cringe mileage from Alan's brazenness but it's pulling from character history rather than constructing something new. Objection/overruled beat that follows is the more comedic part.

dialogue.speaker: AC Repair Student
dialogue.line: I was expelled from the sacred chamber for using it to store my air conditioning supplies on weekends.

jokes.text: You said you were gonna go easy. / Felt easy to me.
jokes.setup: Alan just dragged Shirley through public humiliation about her baby and paternity.
jokes.punchline: 'Felt easy to me' — Alan genuinely considers that restraint.
jokes.explanation: Five-word joke that works entirely on delivery and character. Alan's casual moral vacuum is perfectly captured. Economy score is high — maximum villainy per word.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I'm going to drive you right into unemployment. Driving Miss Daisy style.

jokes.text: What was he wearing? / He was dressed as a dinosaur.
jokes.setup: Britta is probing Evil Abed about his past, presumably asking about childhood memories or formative events.
jokes.punchline: The answer 'He was dressed as a dinosaur' — delivered flatly as if this answers or explains anything — is a perfect non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan absurdism — the total irrelevance and yet total conviction of 'he was dressed as a dinosaur' as a response to what was presumably a serious therapy question is very funny. Brief and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Ted lost the firm he founded because sharks literally ate him.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Well, not literal sharks. I meant it like, you know, sharks in business—cutthroat competitors.

jokes.text: That why you dropped out? / I don't know. / Are those even real glasses? / No. / Ah...
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to therapize Evil Abed and making slow, awkward progress.
jokes.punchline: She asks if his glasses are real (apparently they are not), and his 'No' — combined with her 'Ah...' as if this is a meaningful therapeutic revelation — is funny in its emptiness.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Britta treating 'fake glasses' as a Freudian breakthrough is perfect Britta comedy. The 'Ah...' pause implies she's writing this down as though it means something profound.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How could Ted lose his own firm?

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: The shark metaphor was literal. Ted is dead.

jokes.text: Do you feel that, Britta? Your timeline's 10 percent darker now. / This was 10 percent?
jokes.setup: Evil Abed has been slowly undermining Britta through the therapy session.
jokes.punchline: He announces her timeline is now '10 percent darker' — a comically precise metric for existential damage. Britta's disbelieving 'This was 10 percent?' sells it.
jokes.explanation: The quantification of existential darkness ('10 percent darker') is a great absurdist device, and Britta's reaction ('This was 10 percent?') acknowledges both her own suffering and the comedy of the metric. Good escalation setup.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I am Blind Justice!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Ah! My shin! Why is there a chair here?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Wait, you can see my tattoos? I thought the blindfold was opaque!

jokes.text: Know what kind of person becomes a psychologist? A person that wishes everyone more special than them was sick because 'healthy' sounds more exciting than 'boring.'
jokes.setup: Evil Abed is psychologically attacking Britta by turning her therapy training against her.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a devastating (and somewhat true) critique of people who become psychologists — that they pathologize others to feel special. The logic is mean but coherent.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke that works because it's not purely a dig — it has an internal logic that makes you briefly consider whether it's true. Good character work for both Evil Abed (using psychological insight as a weapon) and Britta (her motivation for studying psych is exactly this).

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Elaborate ceremony and costume

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Casual, annoyed shutdown of over-the-top behavior

jokes.text: You're average, Britta Perry. You're every kid that didn't get picked on. You're a business-casual potted plant, a human white sale. You're VH1, RoboCop 2, and Back to the Future III. The center slice of a square cheese pizza.
jokes.setup: Evil Abed has been building an attack on Britta's identity — she's not exceptional, she's not broken, she's just thoroughly average.
jokes.punchline: The list of 'average' metaphors escalates brilliantly: business-casual potted plant → human white sale → VH1 → RoboCop 2 → Back to the Future III → center slice of a square cheese pizza. Each is more specific and devastating than the last.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the best sustained insult comedies in the series. Each metaphor is carefully chosen: 'business-casual potted plant' (decorative, unremarkable), 'human white sale' (discount, uninspiring but functional), 'VH1' (the worse version of a better thing), 'RoboCop 2' (a sequel nobody asked for), 'Back to the Future III' (the one everyone forgets). The list escalates in pop-culture specificity and each reference is exactly calibrated to mean 'adequate but invisible.' Then 'center slice of a square cheese pizza' as the capstone — not the worst slice, not the best, just the most forgettable. It's a structurally flawless piece of comedic writing. Britta's response ('Sounds delicious') is the perfect comeback, and 'I'm the center slice of a square pizza. You're Jim Belushi' closes it perfectly. Comparable to the Snip Snap anchor in terms of quotability and construction.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's a horrible plan.

dialogue.speaker: Evil Abed
dialogue.line: Dark. It's a dark plan. And welcome to the dark side.

jokes.text: Sounds delicious. / I'm the center slice of a square pizza. You're Jim Belushi.
jokes.setup: Evil Abed calls Britta 'the center slice of a square cheese pizza.'
jokes.punchline: Britta finds the upside ('Sounds delicious') and pivots — 'I'm the center slice of a square pizza. You're Jim Belushi.' The Jim Belushi escalation takes the pizza metaphor and makes it suddenly more brutal — Jim Belushi being the least of the Belushis, riding on name recognition alone.
jokes.explanation: Britta's comeback is as well-constructed as the original attack. 'Sounds delicious' reframes the insult as a compliment (she's comfortable being average), then 'You're Jim Belushi' deploys the same pop-culture-mediocrity logic against her attacker — except Jim Belushi is specifically the person who exists in his more talented sibling's shadow while thinking he deserves more. It's a perfect mirror-reversal of the original joke with an added layer of meaning (Evil Abed IS Abed's shadow). Exceptional economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Everything is terrible. The world is falling apart.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Have you been watching reality TV again?

jokes.text: Ah. Twelve percent.
jokes.setup: Evil Abed has been tracking how much 'darker' the timeline is getting in percentage increments.
jokes.punchline: After being hit with 'You're Jim Belushi,' Evil Abed concedes '12 percent' — implying Britta's comeback actually worked on him, which the percentage metric reveals with perfect economy.
jokes.explanation: Two-word joke. The fact that he went from 10% to 12% — meaning Britta's comeback moved the needle despite his bravado — is revealed with perfect deadpan economy. The running 'darkness percentage' gag pays off brilliantly here because the reader realizes he's been keeping score and her rebuttal scored.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, I stand before you today to deliver a closing argument that will convince you beyond a shadow of a doubt that my client is innocent. I will present irrefutable evidence, logical reasoning, and the kind of legal expertise that you simply cannot argue with.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: However, I've decided to throw this case. Deliberately. I'm going to lose on purpose.

jokes.text: Where are you going? / To make this timeline the darkest. Starting with your lame hero, Jeff Winger. / I don't suppose Lame Abed owns a bone saw.
jokes.setup: Evil Abed declares his intentions and exits.
jokes.punchline: He casually asks if Abed owns a bone saw — implying he intends to cut off Jeff's arm to replicate the darkest timeline — delivered as a practical logistics question.
jokes.explanation: The bone saw question is darkly hilarious — it treats horrifying violence as a practical concern ('do we have the right tool?'). The specificity of 'bone saw' and the mundane framing make this a great dark comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your Honor, I'd like to present a closing argument on behalf of my client...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I'm abandoning this case. My client is guilty as sin.

jokes.text: You're seeking full ownership of Shirley's Sandwiches. After all, you did provide 100 percent of the financing. / Correct. / You really did? / Oh, damn it.
jokes.setup: Jeff is representing Shirley but just had the case framed against him by Alan.
jokes.punchline: The Dean (as judge) asks Pierce to confirm his 100% financing — and Jeff audibly has not researched his own case. 'Oh, damn it' as his self-admitted unpreparedness is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's total unpreparedness played as an in-the-moment realization is good character comedy. His 'Oh, damn it' confession is natural and funny — the great lawyer caught completely off guard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, morality is this complex tapestry of competing philosophical frameworks, existential considerations, and societal paradigms that have evolved over millennia. We have Kant, we have utilitarianism, we have virtue ethics, all wrestling with the fundamental question of what it means to—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Sharing is caring.

jokes.text: Take your time. / Thanks. / Hey, uh, while I'm doing this, anybody know any funny jokes? / I do.
jokes.setup: Jeff is floundering in court, looking at his notes.
jokes.punchline: While the court waits for Jeff, Alan asks if anyone knows 'any funny jokes' — breaking the fourth wall of the courtroom scene with casual informality. Pierce volunteers.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-absurdist moment — a courtroom asking for jokes while waiting for the lawyer to gather himself. It plays with procedural expectations comically.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's the most generic sitcom speech I've ever heard. Next you'll be telling us we all learned something today.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: You're fired, Jeff.

jokes.text: An Irish and a Jew walk into a Chinese laundry with a gay duck. / All right. So you're telling me they're not good at basketball? / I have no questions.
jokes.setup: Pierce tells a joke that starts like a classic multi-ethnic joke setup.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response — 'So you're telling me they're not good at basketball?' — is a deliberately wrong punchline that acknowledges the joke was going nowhere good, and Jeff opts out entirely with 'I have no questions,' using it as an excuse to withdraw his cross-examination.
jokes.explanation: Smart handling of a Pierce racist-joke setup — the show doesn't tell the joke but makes the joke about the joke. Jeff's basketball non-sequitur actively mocks the structure of such jokes while his 'I have no questions' works as a legal punch-out. Good meta-comedy about offensive humor.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I betrayed you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Thank you.

jokes.text: All right. So you're telling me they're not good at basketball? I have no questions.
jokes.setup: Pierce has told his non-punchline joke about an Irish, a Jew, a Chinese laundry, and a gay duck
jokes.punchline: Dean Pelton's takeaway from the joke is 'you're telling me they're not good at basketball?' — an interpretation that makes no sense from the given elements, suggesting he applied his own stereotyping. His 'I have no questions' as a judicial response is an absurd non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Pierce joke. Dean's basketball interpretation comes from nowhere — it's his own stereotyping filling in the absent punchline with something equally nonsensical. 'I have no questions' as a legal ruling on a terrible joke is excellent. The two-joke sequence (#43 + #44) works as a complete comedic unit.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: That's so gay.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Hey, don't use 'gay' as an insult.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Gay is a beautiful thing. I'm a good person.

jokes.text: This ceremony is a lie. And having a special room for it is a waste of floor space. / You are no longer a student here. And we use this room for yoga on weekends.
jokes.setup: Troy challenges the legitimacy of the air conditioning school's ceremonial mysticism.
jokes.punchline: The school dean's response to 'this is a lie' is to both kick Troy out AND reveal they use the sacred ceremonial room for weekend yoga — which retroactively makes the whole thing ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat gag. Troy correctly identifies the cult-like ceremony as false, and the dean's confirming response ('we use this room for yoga on weekends') is a devastating deflation. The yoga reveal strips away all the mystical gravitas of the space in one line.

dialogue.speaker: AC School Leader
dialogue.line: You have committed a terrible crime. You must face our justice.

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: Yeah! Justice! Punishment!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Guys, there's a normal legal system. You're being really weird right now.

jokes.text: I am the truest repairman. Truest repairman. This man is a dishonor to making air conditioners work good.
jokes.setup: A challenger emerges to dispute Troy's destiny claim.
jokes.punchline: 'A dishonor to making air conditioners work good' — the grammatically incorrect 'work good' deflates the epic warrior-cult posturing with casual banality. The solemnity demands 'work well'; 'work good' is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The grammatical slip in an otherwise grandiose speech is a small but effective joke — 'make air conditioners work good' reduces all the mystic grandeur to its mundane core in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That was amazing, Jeff! You were like a young Denzel Washington... if Denzel Washington was white.

jokes.text: Your Less Than Honor, can I call a recess? / Ooh, yay. Costume change. Court briefly adjourned.
jokes.setup: Jeff tries to call a recess to deal with Alan's threat.
jokes.punchline: Jeff addresses the Dean as 'Your Less Than Honor' (a dig at the Dean's credibility as a judge), and the Dean immediately grants the recess purely for 'Costume change' — his judicial duties are entirely secondary to his wardrobe.
jokes.explanation: 'Your Less Than Honor' is a great insult that the Dean doesn't even register. The payoff — he grants the recess only for a costume change — is perfectly in character and funny precisely because his enthusiasm is real.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You should represent both parties.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's actually a good idea, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm going to remember this moment for the rest of your life.

jokes.text: That's right, Jeff. I went there. You drove me there. Miss Daisy's in the house, thanks for the ride, sorry about slavery.
jokes.setup: Alan is making a threat/power play against Jeff during the recess.
jokes.punchline: Alan's victory speech devolves into a Driving Miss Daisy reference ('Miss Daisy's in the house') with the gratuitous 'sorry about slavery' appended — which is so wildly inappropriate it becomes a character-revealing moment for Alan's smarminess.
jokes.explanation: The Driving Miss Daisy escalation with 'sorry about slavery' appended is meant to show Alan's casual racism/insensitivity. It works as character revelation but it's not cleanly constructed as a joke — the punchline leans on the offensive content rather than wit.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm back from AC school, and I think I should be allowed to make the rules now.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I mean, I'm basically a messiah.

jokes.text: Ted respects me. / Ted's gone. Too old. Couldn't swim with sharks and got eaten. / He started the firm. You can't lose your own firm. / You can if you're dead. That shark thing was not a metaphor.
jokes.setup: Jeff invokes Ted (a founding partner) as a check on Alan's power.
jokes.punchline: Alan reveals Ted literally got eaten by sharks — not a metaphor — with the same casual corporate tone used for the rest of the conversation.
jokes.explanation: 'That shark thing was not a metaphor' is a great line — the callback to 'swim with sharks' as literal vs. figurative and Alan's flat correction is well-constructed. The dark corporate-speak masking actual death is both funny and characterful.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I had a psychotic episode in high school.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But I love you guys.

jokes.text: Oh, one more recess. I hit the corner right on a fresh tattoo.
jokes.setup: Court is back in session after the recess; the Dean is in a new outfit.
jokes.punchline: The Dean immediately calls another recess because he has apparently just gotten a new tattoo under his judicial costume, and hitting a corner hurt it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dean Pelton escalation — he barely re-opened court before needing another break for his tattoo. The implication that he got tattooed during the costume change is delightfully absurd. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know, Britta, the fact that you're so fundamentally incompetent at everything is actually really reassuring. Because if you had managed to accidentally cure me, I'd know the universe has gone completely insane.

jokes.text: Well, boys and girls, I hope you brought your popsicles because it's about to get scalding hot in the sun chamber. You already know the rules, because there aren't any!
jokes.setup: The sun chamber duel is about to begin; an announcer hypes it up.
jokes.punchline: 'You already know the rules, because there aren't any!' — a classic action-movie rules announcement that then immediately negates itself.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the action-film announcer trope. The setup ('you know the rules') implies a list is coming; 'because there aren't any' is the clean opposite. Classic misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Welcome back to another episode of Chip Chat. Today we're reviewing the classic Lay's potato chip. Notice the subtle ridge pattern, designed for optimal dipping surface area. The flavor profile is a delicate balance of salt and potato starch. I give it a solid 7 out of 10.

jokes.text: Jeez, Dennis, are you on coke? Take that crap off and sit down.
jokes.setup: An overly theatrical announcer has been building up the sun chamber duel with excessive dramatic energy.
jokes.punchline: He's immediately shut down by his superior, who accuses him of being on cocaine and tells him to sit down — completely puncturing the drama.
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke — the moment of maximum dramatic tension undercut by a superior questioning whether the announcer is on drugs. The name 'Dennis' used casually is a funny choice that makes the institution feel more absurdly real.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: These are adequate potato chips. Crispy, well-salted, good mouthfeel. I'd give them a solid seven out of ten.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: However, this duck-shaped chip changes everything. This is a ten. No, this is an eleven. I'm recommending these chips to everyone I know.

jokes.text: Sorry about that. Of course there are rules. Two men are sealed in the chamber with a broken unit. The heat will increase until one man yields or dies.
jokes.setup: He just apologized for the theatrical excess and promised to describe the actual rules.
jokes.punchline: The 'real rules' turn out to be: die or give up in a death chamber. These are objectively worse and more extreme than 'no rules.' The apology-for-excess followed by an actually extreme description is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good structural reversal — the more 'reasonable' explanation of the rules turns out to describe a literal death trap. The deadpan delivery of 'or dies' makes it land.

jokes.text: Who cares? Everything is terrible. / Oh, no. Have you been watching Dance Moms again? / I'm thinking of dyeing my hair.
jokes.setup: Britta arrives looking dejected after her session with Evil Abed.
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately diagnoses Britta's despair as 'you watched Dance Moms again' — implying this is a known pattern — and Britta's response ('I'm thinking of dyeing my hair') is a classic depression-spiral signal delivered with tragic mundanity.
jokes.explanation: Smart, economical character beat. 'Have you been watching Dance Moms again' as Shirley's immediate read on Britta's existential despair is funny and character-specific. The hair-dyeing response as a cry-for-help signal is relatable and well-timed.

jokes.text: What are you doing? / Going to cut off Winger's arm. / That's horrible. / Don't you mean dark? / Welcome to my world.
jokes.setup: Britta asks what Evil Abed is doing as he heads out.
jokes.punchline: He corrects 'horrible' to 'dark' — asserting a preferred vocabulary for his villainy — and 'Welcome to my world' as his goodbye is delivered with complete villain sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The vocabulary correction ('don't you mean dark?') is a great character moment — a villain insisting on his own brand. 'Welcome to my world' is Abed-as-character fully committing to the bit. Good economy.

jokes.text: Your Honor, I have no closing statement because I'm throwing the case. / No, no, it's okay. It's fine, don't worry.
jokes.setup: Jeff is about to deliver a closing statement in the mock trial.
jokes.punchline: He announces he's throwing the case — then immediately tries to reassure everyone that this is fine before anyone has even reacted.
jokes.explanation: The setup-then-immediate-reassurance structure is funny but this is primarily a dramatic beat with a comedic entrance. Functions more as the launch of Jeff's speech than a complete joke.

jokes.text: I'll kill you. I'll kill you just like I killed him. / Was that out loud?
jokes.setup: Jeff is making his speech about how 'guys like me can never lose' — implicitly calling out Alan during his closing statement.
jokes.punchline: Alan audibly threatens to kill Jeff, then immediately asks 'Was that out loud?' — a standard 'thought I was thinking that' gag elevated by the content being a murder confession.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The 'was that out loud?' gag is a familiar structure, but its execution here is exceptional: it's a villain accidentally confessing to murder in a courtroom during someone else's inspirational speech, and his only response is to wonder if it was audible. The structure builds perfectly — Jeff is making a sincere speech, Alan is seething, the murder confession erupts, and 'Was that out loud?' is the perfect deflation. High economy, high impact.

jokes.text: Why didn't you just do some inspirational speech about friendship? / You're fired.
jokes.setup: Alan lost the case due to Jeff's speech and Pierce withdrew his claim.
jokes.punchline: Alan sarcastically asks why Jeff did 'an inspirational speech about friendship' — then Pierce immediately fires Alan, the punchline being that Alan's sarcasm got him fired.
jokes.explanation: Good structural gag — Alan's dismissive sarcasm triggers the exact outcome he feared (losing Pierce as a client). The instantaneousness of 'You're fired' after the eye-roll is clean comedy.

jokes.text: Well, way to go, soft serve. You're finished. By the way, never got a chance to tell you this, but it was me who turned you in to the State Bar. / I know. And I never got a chance to thank you.
jokes.setup: Alan gloats that Jeff is finished, then reveals he was the one who turned Jeff in to the State Bar — presumably expecting devastation.
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds 'I know. And I never got a chance to thank you' — the anticipated devastation reversed into gratitude, because Greendale changed Jeff for the better.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'thank you' is both the comedic punchline and the thematic statement of the episode. It lands as a great joke because it completely wrong-foots Alan, and as a character moment because it's true — being disbarred led Jeff to Greendale, which made him a better person. The best jokes here do double duty as character revelation, and this is one of them.

jokes.text: This place has made you so gay. / Hey. Don't use 'gay' as a derogatory term. / Boo-yah. Good person.
jokes.setup: Alan insults Jeff's growth as 'gay'; Jeff immediately calls it out.
jokes.punchline: Shirley punctuates Jeff's correction with 'Boo-yah. Good person.' — treating Jeff's objection as a teachable moment she can claim credit for.
jokes.explanation: Shirley's 'Boo-yah. Good person.' is a great quick beat — she claims Jeff's moral growth as her own victory. The rhythm is excellent and it's a character-specific reaction.

jokes.text: Take this man to the infinite labyrinth of eternal ice. / Yeah! / No. Take him to the police. He murdered someone. / Take him to jail. / You guys are weird.
jokes.setup: The villain of the AC school has just confessed to murder.
jokes.punchline: The school dean wants to send him to their own punitive system ('the infinite labyrinth of eternal ice'); Troy briefly cheers this; Jeff and others insist on the actual police instead. The villain's reaction to all this is 'You guys are weird.'
jokes.explanation: The clash between the AC school's elaborate fantasy punishment ('infinite labyrinth of eternal ice') and normal reality ('take him to the police') is a great deflation joke. 'You guys are weird' as the villain's final word is a perfect inversion — the murderer calling the heroes weird.

jokes.text: Jeff, that was great. You were a white Blair Underwood.
jokes.setup: Everyone is congratulating Jeff on his speech.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's compliment — 'You were a white Blair Underwood' — is funny because Blair Underwood is a Black actor known for legal dramas, making Shirley's racialized compliment absurd and very Shirley-ish.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specificity of 'white Blair Underwood' — it's simultaneously a compliment and an oddly racially-framed one that reveals more about Shirley than Jeff. Character-specific but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Shirley, we should let Jeff sign the sandwich shop form. You could represent us, like our attorney. My God, Pierce. You had your first good idea.
jokes.setup: Pierce suggests Jeff be their attorney by signing the form
jokes.punchline: Shirley's 'My God, Pierce. You had your first good idea.' — a compliment framed as a statistical miracle, implying Pierce's track record with ideas is so bad that one good one is newsworthy
jokes.explanation: Classic Community group dynamic joke. 'Your first good idea' implies a long history of terrible Pierce ideas, which is accurate characterization. Functional and character-appropriate but not exceptional.

jokes.text: But you can't. You cured me. / I'm not cured. I'm willing to admit I need therapy. / You're the only kind of shrink I trust. The kind with as little control over my mind as me.
jokes.setup: Britta says she should change her major again (away from psychology) after her failed session with Abed.
jokes.punchline: Abed clarifies he's 'not cured' but willing to seek therapy — then endorses Britta as 'the kind of shrink with as little control over my mind as me,' which is simultaneously sincere, insulting, and oddly sweet.
jokes.explanation: One of the more emotionally resonant jokes in the episode — Abed's endorsement of Britta as a therapist is technically a devastating critique of her skills, but it functions as genuine affection. The logic is very Abed and the line is quotable in the context of the show.

jokes.text: You're back. / Yeah. Made a rule that the air conditioning repair school has to act like a regular school. I can do that. I'm their messiah.
jokes.setup: Troy has returned from the AC school.
jokes.punchline: His explanation for being able to leave: 'I made a rule. I can do that. I'm their messiah.' Delivered with total casual confidence.
jokes.explanation: Troy's completely nonchalant 'I'm their messiah' as an administrative fact is a great character beat. The whole prophesy arc pays off in a one-liner that Troy doesn't even consider remarkable.

jokes.text: Cool. I went crazy and I wanted to cut off Jeff's arm. / I missed you so much, buddy.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are reuniting after their separation.
jokes.punchline: Abed's reunion update is 'I went crazy and I wanted to cut off Jeff's arm' — delivered as a normal conversational update. Troy's response is pure warmth without addressing the content at all.
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier joke in the episode. Abed's flat-affect summary of his entire psychological crisis ('I went crazy and I wanted to cut off Jeff's arm') delivered as a casual update, followed by Troy's total non-engagement ('I missed you so much, buddy'), captures the Troy-and-Abed dynamic perfectly. The economy is superb, the character integration is complete, and the contrast between the horrifying content and the warmth of Troy's response is emotionally and comedically perfect.

jokes.text: So, Jeff, are we still best friends? [long pause]
jokes.setup: Pierce has been kind to Jeff by withdrawing his case, and apparently believes this has forged a deep bond.
jokes.punchline: Pierce sincerely asks Jeff if they're 'still best friends' — implying he considers them that — and the ensuing silence/reaction beat (inferred from [15+ second gap before next dialogue]) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The gap between Pierce asking this and the next line of dialogue ([19:23] resuming with mitosis) suggests a long, awkward silence that is entirely the joke. Pierce's earnestness about best-friendship with Jeff, and Jeff's evident inability to answer, is classic Pierce-Jeff comedy.

jokes.text: Hello, everybody. I'm Leonard. I'm here today to review Let's Potato Chips.
jokes.setup: Post-credits tag: Leonard is apparently running a YouTube/online review channel.
jokes.punchline: The discovery that Leonard does casual chip reviews as an ongoing activity — delivered in his oblivious, cheerful register — is funny as a character revelation and a parody of online review culture.
jokes.explanation: The Leonard post-credits sequence is a great standalone bit. The concept (this 70+ year-old curmudgeon has a YouTube channel) is perfect, and his review methodology (he's already eaten some, he opens another bag, finds a duck-shaped chip) is pitch-perfect parody. Good character integration.

jokes.text: See if I can get this sucker open. Ha. There we are. Now... I've already had some of these, but let's see. Mm, crispy. Thanks for doing the dishes. Salty, not too greasy. Ha, ha. That one is shaped like a duck. Ha, ha.
jokes.setup: Leonard reviews the chips with the gravity of a professional product critic.
jokes.punchline: His 'review' consists of: struggling to open the bag, noting they're 'crispy,' a non-sequitur 'thanks for doing the dishes,' noting they're 'salty not too greasy,' and finding a duck-shaped chip — none of which constitutes useful consumer information.
jokes.explanation: 'Thanks for doing the dishes' mid-review is the standout moment here — an inexplicable aside that implies Leonard is talking to someone off-camera, breaking the reviewer frame completely. The duck-shaped chip getting its own 'ha, ha' is also excellent. The whole sequence rewards watching Leonard as a character.

jokes.text: Mm, crispy. Thanks for doing the dishes. Salty, not too greasy. Ha, ha. That one is shaped like a duck. Ha, ha. Well, I guess that's definitely a buy.
jokes.setup: Leonard is reviewing the chips, eating them and providing notes
jokes.punchline: 'Thanks for doing the dishes' is a non-sequitur mid-review, apparently said to someone off-camera — revealing that Leonard has an audience for this production (housekeeper? family member?) while also being completely irrelevant to the chip review. 'That one is shaped like a duck' as a review criterion is also excellent.
jokes.explanation: Several good jokes in rapid succession. 'Thanks for doing the dishes' mid-review is a perfect non-sequitur that reveals the texture of Leonard's domestic life mid-performance. 'That one is shaped like a duck' as a consumer product evaluation is an excellent absurdist detail — chip shape is not a standard review criterion. 'Ha, ha' repeated twice is the right deadpan vocal laugh. The whole sequence has an organic, authentic comedy that is funnier than it looks on paper.

jokes.text: Let's Potato Chips are good and they're a buy. ♪ I'm as high as hell and you're about to get shot ♪
jokes.setup: Leonard wraps up his review with a professional conclusion ('a buy').
jokes.punchline: The end card music that plays over Leonard's review is a song with the lyrics 'I'm as high as hell and you're about to get shot' — a wildly inappropriate outro for a chip review.
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the episode and a great one. Leonard's earnest, wholesome chip review ends with an outro song about being high and threatening to shoot someone. The contrast is maximized by how well the professional review format was established — this pulls the rug perfectly. It's a pure tonal whiplash joke with excellent economy.

tmdb_overview: Jeff agrees to represent Shirley in a case against Pierce to determine official ownership of their new sandwich shop.
insight: Season finale escalates absurdist chaos to 81.8, delivering 2.64 jokes per minute across 58 gags.
